Source slide page 3 (extracted text):
PYTHON FOR COMPUTATIONAL PROBLEM SOLVING
 Tuple

Tuple is a data structure containing zero or more elements.

 Creation of tuple

  •  An empty tuple can be created using a constructor,
        tuplep   ()() or ().()
  •  Tuple with two elements.
         t3 = (1, 2)
  •  Tuple with a single element.
         t3=(1,)

Source slide page 4 (extracted text):
PYTHON FOR COMPUTATIONAL PROBLEM SOLVING
 Tuple

• Each element of a tuple can be referred to by a index or a subscript.
• Index is an integer.
Ex:
       >>> t1=(11,22,33,44,55)
       >>> t1[1]
          22
       >>> t1[-1]
           55

Source slide page 5 (extracted text):
PYTHON FOR COMPUTATIONAL PROBLEM SOLVING
 Tuple


 • Tuples are immutable. Once created, we cannot change the number of elements
 – no append, no insert, no remove, no delete.



>>> z = (5, 4, 3)
>>> z[2] = 0

Traceback:'tuple' object does not support item

Assignment

Source slide page 6 (extracted text):
PYTHON FOR COMPUTATIONAL PROBLEM SOLVING
 Tuple

Benefits of usage of type - Tuple:
• Tuples are faster than lists.
•  If the user wants to protect the data from accidental changes, tuple can be used.
• Tuples can be used as keys in dictionaries, while lists can't.

Source slide page 7 (extracted text):
PYTHON FOR COMPUTATIONAL PROBLEM SOLVING
 Tuple


• Elements in the tuple can repeat .

       >>> t1=(11,22,33,44,22,11,55)

• Tuple is a sequence .
• Tuple is also iterable - is eager and not lazy.
         t2=(5,10,15,20)
         for i in t2:
                    print(i, end=' ‘)
• Tuples can be nested. We can have tuple of tuples.
          t=(1,2,3,4,(6,7,8))
         for i in t:
                    print(i)

  Common errors and good practices

The Translation Crash: JSON is very basic and only understands simple things like text, numbers,
and lists. It has no idea what a Python date, set, or custom object is. If you try to save them directly,
your code will crash. You must simplify them first: turn dates into text strings, and turn sets into
normal lists.

The Sneaky Key Change: Python lets you use numbers as dictionary keys (like {1: "apple"}). JSON
absolutely refuses this and only allows text keys. It will quietly change your number 1 into a text string
"1" without warning you. When you load your data back into Python, you might get bugs because your
numbers are now text.

The Broken Data Trap: Never blindly trust a JSON file from the internet or a user. If the file is
missing even a single comma or quote, your entire program will instantly crash when it tries to read it.
Always wrap your code in a try/except block so it catches the error instead of breaking your app.

Ugly Text Syndrome: By default, JSON is terrified of accents and special characters. It will take a
word like "café" and scramble it into ugly machine code like caf\u00e9. To force it to leave your text
alone and keep it readable, you have to tell it ensure_ascii=False when you save the data.

The Windows vs. Mac Glitch: Different computers assume different default text formats when
opening files. If you do not specify a format, moving a JSON file between computers can scramble the
text. Always  explicitly write encoding="utf-8" inside your open() function to guarantee  it works
flawlessly everywhere.
